statement:
Assume full AC. Fix $m\ge1$, $2<q<4$, and $q^*=4q/(4-q)$. There are constants $\delta=\delta(m,q)>0$ and finite constants $K_2=K_2(m)$ and $K_q=K_q(m,q)$, having the following property. Let $B:\mathbb R^4\to\operatorname{Hom}(\mathbb R^{4m},\mathbb R^m)$ be measurable, compactly supported and $\|B\|_4\le\delta$, where the pointwise norm is the operator norm. Let $f\in L^2(\mathbb R^4;\mathbb R^m)\cap L^q(\mathbb R^4;\mathbb R^m)$ be compactly supported. Set
$$\Phi(x)=\frac{1}{4\pi^2|x|^2},\qquad Nv=\Phi*v,\qquad Hv=\nabla Nv,$$
with the pole value chosen arbitrarily and all expressions interpreted as almost-everywhere classes. There is a unique $w\in L^4(\mathbb R^4;\mathbb R^{4m})$ satisfying
$$w=H(f+Bw).$$
It also belongs to $L^{q^*}$, satisfies $\|w\|_4\le2K_2\|f\|_2$ and $\|w\|_{q^*}\le2K_q\|f\|_q$, and is the gradient of
$$u=N(f+Bw)\in W^{2,q}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^4;\mathbb R^m),\qquad -\Delta u=f+B\nabla u.$$
The fixed point is the limit of $w_0=0$, $w_{j+1}=H(f+Bw_j)$ in both indicated gradient norms.

Consequently any compactly supported $v\in W^{1,2}(\mathbb R^4;\mathbb R^m)$ with $\nabla v\in L^4$ satisfying $-\Delta v=f+B\nabla v$ distributionally equals this $u$ almost everywhere and belongs to $W^{2,q}_{\mathrm{loc}}$. The smallness threshold is independent of the diameter of the supports: for the dilation $x=ry$, the transformed drift is $B_r(y)=rB(ry)$ and $\|B_r\|_4=\|B\|_4$.

steps.text: **The potential for smooth data.** Fix $s\in\{2,q\}$ and initially $v\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^4;\mathbb R^m)$ supported in $B_R$. The formula $Nv(x)=\int\Phi(y)v(x-y)\,dy$ permits differentiation of $v$ under the integral on every bounded set, since $\Phi$ is locally integrable and all relevant $y$ lie in a bounded set. Thus $Nv$ is smooth, with $-\Delta Nv=v$ by [F1]. Differentiating the kernel off the support gives $|D^kNv(x)|\le C_k\|v\|_1|x|^{-2-k}$ for $|x|>2R$ and $k=0,1$. Choose a fixed smooth cutoff $\chi=1$ on $B_1$ supported in $B_2$ and put $\chi_T(x)=\chi(x/T)$. For $T>2R$, $\Delta(\chi_TNv)=-v+2\nabla\chi_T\cdot\nabla Nv+(\Delta\chi_T)Nv$, and the last two terms have $L^s$ norm at most $C\|v\|_1T^{-4+4/s}$, which tends to zero. [F1, F4, given, construct, algebra]

**Global Hessians without a low-frequency inverse assumption.** Apply the first estimate of [F2] to the smooth compactly supported $\chi_TNv$. On any fixed ball it equals $Nv$ for large $T$, so step 1.1 gives $\|D^2Nv\|_{L^s(B_M)}\le C_s\|v\|_s$ after taking $T\to\infty$. Increasing $M$ to infinity by [F4] yields $\|D^2Nv\|_s\le C_s\|v\|_s$, with the Euclidean norm on the finitely many Hessian coefficients absorbed into $C_s$. This argument uses a compactly supported function in the global estimate, rather than assuming that $Nv$ itself lies in global $W^{2,s}$. [F2, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

**General compactly supported data.** For compactly supported $v\in L^s$, [F4] gives smooth $v_j	o v$ in $L^s$ with supports in one fixed ball; hence also $v_j	o v$ in $L^1$ by [F3]. On each bounded target ball, convolution with the restrictions of $\Phi$ and $
abla\Phi$ to a sufficiently large ball is bounded on $L^s$ by Young's inequality: both kernels are locally integrable in four dimensions. Thus $Nv_j	o Nv$ and $
abla Nv_j	o
abla Nv$ in $L^s_{\mathrm{loc}}$, with the latter identification also following from the distributional derivative test identity. Step 2.1 on differences makes $D^2Nv_j$ Cauchy in global $L^s$; completeness and passage in the weak-derivative test identity identify its limit as $D^2Nv$. Therefore $Nv\in W^{2,s}_{\mathrm{loc}}$ and $\|D^2Nv\|_s\le C_s\|v\|_s$. Moreover $
abla Nv\in L^s(\mathbb R^4)$: the local Young estimate handles a ball containing the support, and the off-support bound $|
abla Nv(x)|\le C\|v\|_1|x|^{-3}$ handles its complement, since $s>4/3$. Hence each component of $Hv=
abla Nv$ belongs to global $W^{1,s}$. [F1, F3, F4, step 2.1, algebra]

**The two consistent gradient bounds.** The second estimate of [F2] applied to each component of $Hv$ in step 3.1 gives $\|Hv\|_{s^*}\le K_s\|v\|_s$, where $s^*=4s/(4-s)$ and $K_s$ depends only on $m,s$, not on the support radius. When $v$ lies in both source spaces, these operators are the same distributional gradient of the same convolution, so their output classes agree. This proves bounded maps from compactly supported $L^2$ to $L^4$ and from compactly supported $L^q$ to $L^{q^*}$ with consistent values. [F2, step 3.1, algebra]

**Two contractions with the same iterates.** Choose $\delta=(2\max\{K_2,K_q\})^{-1}$. Since $1/2=1/4+1/4$ and $1/q=1/4+1/q^*$, Holder [F3] gives $\|Bz\|_2\le\delta\|z\|_4$ and $\|Bz\|_q\le\delta\|z\|_{q^*}$. The products are supported in the fixed compact support of $B$, so $Tz=H(f+Bz)$ is defined on each of the complete spaces $L^4$ and $L^{q^*}$. Step 4.1 makes its contraction constant at most $1/2$ in each space. Starting with zero, all iterates lie in their intersection, and [F3] gives convergence in both spaces. [F3, step 4.1, choose, construct]

**Identification, estimates and uniqueness.** On every bounded ball, either gradient-norm convergence from step 5.1 implies $L^1$ convergence by Holder. Hence the two limits define the same distribution and the same almost-everywhere class $w$. The fixed point equation in both spaces and step 4.1 yield $\|w\|_4\le K_2\|f\|_2+\tfrac12\|w\|_4$ and $\|w\|_{q^*}\le K_q\|f\|_q+\tfrac12\|w\|_{q^*}$, giving the stated estimates. Any $L^4$ fixed point is this $w$, by the contraction uniqueness in [F3]. [F3, step 4.1, step 5.1, algebra]

**An actual potential solution.** The class $s_0=f+Bw$ is compactly supported and lies in $L^2\cap L^q$ by steps 5.1–5.1. Set $u=Ns_0$. Step 3.1 gives $u\in W^{2,q}_{\mathrm{loc}}$, the fixed point equation gives $\nabla u=w$, and [F1] gives $-\Delta u=s_0=f+B\nabla u$ distributionally. This is an existence construction, with the Newtonian normalization specified in the statement. [F1, step 3.1, step 5.1, step 6.1, construct]

**Identification of compactly supported weak solutions.** Let $v$ be as in the consequent clause and put $s_1=f+B
abla v\in L^2_c$. By [F1], $v-Ns_1$ is distributionally harmonic on all of $\mathbb R^4$, so [F5] gives a smooth entire harmonic representative. Outside a ball containing the supports, $v=0$ almost everywhere and $Ns_1=O(|x|^{-2})$ directly from the kernel formula and $s_1\in L^1_c$. The harmonic representative therefore tends to zero at infinity; equality almost everywhere there is equality everywhere with the smooth off-support potential. It is bounded on the remaining compact ball, so [F5] makes it identically zero. Thus $v=Ns_1$, whence $
abla v=H(f+B
abla v)$ is an $L^4$ fixed point. Step 6.1 gives $
abla v=w$, so $s_1=s_0$ and $v=u$; step 7.1 proves the asserted regularity. [F1, F3, F5, step 6.1, step 7.1, algebra]

**Scaling and choice.** For $u_r(y)=u(ry)$, direct differentiation gives $-\Delta_yu_r=r^2f(ry)+rB(ry)\nabla_yu_r$. The four-dimensional change of variables gives $\|rB(r\cdot)\|_4=\|B\|_4$, while both $\|\nabla u_r\|_{q^*}$ and $\|r^2f(r\cdot)\|_q$ scale by $r^{2-4/q}$, and the analogous $L^4/L^2$ factors are one. The constants in step 4.1 are whole-space constants, so $\delta$ is independent of the compact supports. Full AC is inherited only through [F2] and the countable analytic selections in [F3]–[F6]. [F2, F3, F4, F6, step 4.1, step 5.1, step 7.1, step 8.1, algebra] ∎

statement:
Assume full AC. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^4$ be open. Let $a,b\in L^4_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathfrak{su}(2)\otimes\mathbb R^4)$ satisfy $\sum_i\partial_i a_i=\sum_i\partial_i b_i=0$ distributionally. Suppose $h\in W^{1,2}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb C^{2\times2})$ takes values in $SU(2)$ almost everywhere and satisfies the transition equation
$$\partial_i h=hb_i-a_i h\qquad(i=1,\ldots,4)$$
distributionally. Then $h\in W^{2,q}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ for every $2<q<4$ and has a unique continuous representative $h^*:\Omega\to SU(2)$, locally $C^{0,\alpha}$ for every $0<\alpha<1$.

For a finite open cover with given Coulomb forms $a_i$ and transition classes $h_{ij}$ satisfying these hypotheses on overlaps, any almost-everywhere identities $h_{ii}=1$, $h_{ji}=h_{ij}^{-1}$ and $h_{ij}h_{jk}=h_{ik}$ hold everywhere for the continuous representatives. Thus they form a continuous transition cocycle on the same open overlaps. Likewise any given almost-everywhere finite equivariance identities $h(\gamma x)=\rho(\gamma)^{-1}h(x)\rho(\gamma)$, for $\Gamma\le O(4)$ preserving $\Omega$ and a representation $\rho:\Gamma\to SU(2)$, hold pointwise for $h^*$.

The regularity assertions are interior assertions on smaller balls compactly contained in $\Omega$. No condition or regularity at $\partial\Omega$, no construction of a Coulomb gauge from curvature, and no existence of equivariant gauges is assumed or concluded.

steps.text: **The first derivative already has critical integrability.** An $SU(2)$ matrix is unitary, hence has fixed Frobenius norm $\sqrt2$. Matrix multiplication obeys $|XY|\le|X||Y|$. The transition equation therefore gives $|\nabla h|\le\sqrt2(|a|+|b|)$ almost everywhere, with the Euclidean coefficient norms. Thus $h\in W^{1,4}_{\mathrm{loc}}$, as well as being locally bounded. [F2, given, algebra]

**The drift equation is valid for weak Coulomb forms.** The distributional identity $\sum_i\partial_i b_i=0$ extends to compactly supported $W^{1,4/3}$ matrix tests by Holder and smooth approximation [F2]–[F3]. In particular one may test with products of a smooth test and an entry of $h$, since $h\in W^{1,4}_{\mathrm{loc}}$ and is bounded. Expanding the derivative of this product gives $\sum_i\partial_i(hb_i)=\sum_i(\partial_i h)b_i$ distributionally; applying the same argument to $a$ gives $\sum_i\partial_i(a_i h)=\sum_i a_i\partial_i h$. These expansions can also be obtained by approximating $h$ in $W^{1,4}$ on the compact test support, with a fixed cutoff, and taking limits of all pairings by Holder. Differentiating the transition equation now gives $-\Delta h=\sum_i(a_i\partial_i h-(\partial_i h)b_i)=B\nabla h$, where $B(x)(v)=\sum_i(a_i(x)v_i-v_i b_i(x))$. Viewing complex $2\times2$ matrices as $\mathbb R^8$, Cauchy–Schwarz and the matrix product bound give $|B(x)|_{\mathrm{op}}\le|a(x)|+|b(x)|$. [F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

**Localization makes the drift small.** For each $x\in\Omega$, choose a ball $B_R(x)$ compactly contained in $\Omega$. Absolute continuity [F2] applied to $(|a|+|b|)^4$ on this ball gives $0<r<R/2$ so small that $\|B\|_{L^4(B_{2r}(x))}\le\delta(8,q)$. Choose $\chi\in C_c^\infty(B_{2r}(x))$ equal to one on a neighbourhood of $\overline B_r(x)$ by [F3]. Extend $u=\chi h$ by zero to $\mathbb R^4$; it is compactly supported and in $W^{1,4}$, hence in $W^{1,2}$ with $L^4$ gradient. Extend $B|_{B_{2r}(x)}$ by zero as $\widetilde B$. The weak Leibniz rule and step 2.1 give $-\Delta u=\widetilde B\nabla u+f$, where inside $B_{2r}(x)$ one sets $f=-B(h\,d\chi)-2\sum_i(\partial_i\chi)(\partial_i h)-(\Delta\chi)h$ and outside sets $f=0$. All terms are supported in a compact subset of this ball and belong to $L^4$, by boundedness of $h$, local $L^4$ integrability of $B,\nabla h$, and smoothness of the cutoff. Therefore $f\in L^2_c\cap L^q_c$ by Holder. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, choose, construct, algebra]

**Application of the constructed inverse.** The coefficient $\widetilde B$ is compactly supported with $L^4$ norm at most $\delta(8,q)$, and step 3.1 verifies every hypothesis of [F1]. It follows that $u\in W^{2,q}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^4)$; since $u=h$ near $\overline B_r(x)$, the same holds for $h$ near $x$. Repeating at every $x$ proves $h\in W^{2,q}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$: every compact subset is covered by finitely many such smaller balls, and integrals of the weak derivatives over it are bounded by the sum over that finite cover. The exponent $q$ was arbitrary in $(2,4)$. [F1, step 3.1, algebra]

**Representatives and the group constraint.** For any $0<\alpha<1$, choose $q\in(2,4)$ with $\alpha<2-4/q$. On each smaller ball step 4.1 and [F4] give a $C^{0,\alpha}$ representative. Two such continuous representatives agree everywhere on their open overlap: their difference vanishes almost everywhere, whereas a nonzero value of a continuous difference persists on an open ball of positive Lebesgue measure. Thus these local representatives define a unique continuous $h^*$ on $\Omega$, locally $C^{0,\alpha}$ for every $\alpha<1$. Since $SU(2)$ is closed in the matrix space (it is given by $H^*H=1$ and $\det H=1$), a continuous representative equal to an $SU(2)$-valued class almost everywhere takes its values in $SU(2)$ everywhere, by the same positive-measure argument. [F4, step 4.1, choose, algebra]

**Cocycle and equivariance patching.** Matrix multiplication and inversion on $SU(2)$ are continuous. On any open triple overlap, $h^*_{ij}h^*_{jk}-h^*_{ik}$ is continuous and zero almost everywhere, so the argument of step 5.1 makes it zero everywhere. The identities for $h_{ii}$ and $h_{ji}$ follow in the same way, giving the asserted continuous transition cocycle. Orthogonal changes of variables preserve Lebesgue null sets. Consequently $h^*(\gamma x)$ and $\rho(\gamma)^{-1}h^*(x)\rho(\gamma)$ are continuous representatives of the two almost-everywhere equal classes in any given equivariance identity; uniqueness makes them equal at every $x$. This applies to each element of the given finite group. [step 5.1, given, algebra]

**Conclusion and boundaries of use.** Steps 4.1–6.1 prove all regularity, cocycle and equivariance assertions. Every cutoff was supported strictly inside $\Omega$; no trace or boundary condition was used. The input transition equation and the input Coulomb forms were assumed, and the proof constructs compatible continuous representatives of those transitions, with no assertion that gauges producing those forms exist. Full AC is used through the explicitly identified suppliers [F1], [F3]–[F5]. [F1, F3, F4, F5, step 4.1, step 5.1, step 6.1] ∎
